verses.text: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered,
“Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself.
Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that you are righteous? Or does it benefit him, that you make your ways perfect?
Is it for your piety that he reproves you, that he enters with you into judgment?
Isn’t your wickedness great? Neither is there any end to your iniquities.
For you have taken pledges from your brother for nothing, and stripped the naked of their clothing.
You haven’t given water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry.
But as for the mighty man, he had the earth. The honorable man, he lived in it.
You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken.
Therefore snares are around you. Sudden fear troubles you,
or darkness, so that you can not see, and floods of waters cover you.
“Isn’t God in the heights of heaven? See the height of the stars, how high they are!
You say, ‘What does God know? Can he judge through the thick darkness?
Thick clouds are a covering to him, so that he doesn’t see. He walks on the vault of the sky.’
Will you keep the old way, which wicked men have trodden,
who were snatched away before their time, whose foundation was poured out as a stream,
who said to God, ‘Depart from us;’ and, ‘What can the Almighty do for us?’
Yet he filled their houses with good things, but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.
The righteous see it, and are glad. The innocent ridicule them,
saying, ‘Surely those who rose up against us are cut off. The fire has consumed their remnant.’
“Acquaint yourself with him, now, and be at peace. Thereby good shall come to you.
Please receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart.
If you return to the Almighty, you shall be built up, if you put away unrighteousness far from your tents.
Lay your treasure in the dust, the gold of Ophir among the stones of the brooks.
The Almighty will be your treasure, and precious silver to you.
For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty, and shall lift up your face to God.
You shall make your prayer to him, and he will hear you. You shall pay your vows.
You shall also decree a thing, and it shall be established to you. Light shall shine on your ways.
When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.
He will even deliver him who is not innocent. Yes, he shall be delivered through the cleanness of your hands.”

footnotes.content: Eliphaz speaks again, and his tone has shifted—no longer gentle comfort but hard accusation. This is where a 'friend' becomes an adversary, convinced he knows the secret sin Job is hiding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphaz begins with a false first principle: God profits nothing from our righteousness. But this misses grace entirely—the Father's joy is in His children themselves, not in what they produce for Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Another corrupted idea: that God reproves us because we're righteous. No—the Lord reproves those He loves, yes, but out of costly care, never coldly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphaz slides from theology to trial: surely God is prosecuting you now because of your piety? He has it backwards. The question itself is the mirror: what drives him to such certainty that Job must be guilty?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now come the accusations—wickedness great, iniquities endless. Eliphaz speaks with utter confidence. How often do we do the same, filling in the missing pieces of someone's story with our own suspicions?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pledges from brothers, stripping the naked—concrete charges. The law protected both; Exodus 22:26–27 forbade keeping a neighbor's cloak overnight. But Eliphaz speaks from assumption, not evidence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Withholding water and bread—the marks of cruelty to the vulnerable. Yet we never hear Job's side. Job's own mouth will tell us his heart toward the hungry and thirsty; this chapter is the poison of hearsay.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mighty inhabited the land, the honorable lived in it. Eliphaz may mean: while wicked men ruled, where was justice? Or he means Job curried favor with the powerful. Either way, it's a non-sequitur.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Widows sent away empty, fatherless with broken arms—the language of ancient cruelty toward the defenseless. Eliphaz is thorough in his indictment, painting Job as a man of stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Therefore snares, sudden fear. This is Eliphaz's answer to Job's lament: you fear because you are guilty. To the sufferer, this sounds like: your fear proves your guilt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Darkness, floods covering—the very words Job himself has used to describe his trial. Eliphaz takes Job's own testimony and weaponizes it as proof of judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Eliphaz shifts: he reminds Job that God is high, exalted. But notice—he's about to use this to prove God *can't* see Job's guilt clearly. The exaltation becomes distance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphaz quotes the wicked: 'What does God know?' He's putting evil words on Job, saying: this is what your suffering tells me you believe. It's a dangerous thing to put words in another's mouth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thick clouds hide God from seeing; He walks the vault blindly. Eliphaz invents a distant, negligent God to frame his accusation. Job does not believe this. But Eliphaz needs Job to seem godless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Will you keep the old way? Eliphaz wants Job to repent of a wickedness he has not committed, to confess a sin that exists only in Eliphaz's mind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those men—snatched before their time, foundation poured out like water. Eliphaz knows the pattern of judgment and names it. What he doesn't know is whether it fits Job.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Depart from us'—the cry of the godless. Yet Job has never said this. Eliphaz is constructing a portrait of Job as an outright rebel, a man who wants no part of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet he filled their houses with good—God even blessed the wicked with prosperity before judgment fell. Eliphaz acknowledges the mystery but uses it to trap Job: if you suffer, you must be wicked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The righteous see and are glad, the innocent ridicule them. Eliphaz suggests that everyone can see Job's guilt except Job. This too is a weapon: conformity as proof.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who rose up against us are cut off—Eliphaz speaks as if Job's suffering proves he rose up against God. Mercy has its limits in this theology, and Job has run past them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the accusations, the counsel: acquaint yourself with God and be at peace. If only it were so simple—as if repenting of imagined sin could undo real mystery.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Receive instruction from his mouth—but whose? Eliphaz has been doing the instructing, putting words on God that God has not spoken. This is the trap of the comforter: the words taste true until they don't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Return to the Almighty, be built up, put away unrighteousness. This is the promise—but it assumes Job has strayed. What if he has not? Then this verse becomes a cruel lie.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lay your treasure in dust, gold of Ophir among stones—Ophir was a distant land of wealth (1 Kings 9:28). Eliphaz counsels renunciation: strip yourself of possessions as a sign of repentance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Almighty will be your treasure—a promise of sufficiency, of God Himself as the end of longing. Beautiful words, but they sting when they presume the hearer has turned from God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You will delight yourself in the Almighty—the very joy Job craves. Eliphaz dangles the answer, unaware that Job has not lost delight in God; he has lost the sense of being held by God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Make your prayer and he will hear—the promise of answered prayer. Pay your vows. And yet Eliphaz speaks as if Job has broken faith with God, when Job's complaint is that God seems to have broken faith with him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You shall decree and it shall be established, light shall shine—prosperity and clarity shall return. Eliphaz ends on a golden note: repent and all will be restored. If only human suffering worked this way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When they cast down, say be lifted up. He will save the humble. Eliphaz believes in inversion—cast down becomes lifted up if only you confess. This theology breaks when the humble are also cast down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this final word—even if you are not innocent, the innocent shall deliver you through clean hands. It hints at an ancient mystery: one can stand in the place of another. The Lord Jesus, innocent and clean-handed, stood there for all of us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
